$comment: Static-analysis findings a person has read and accepted as not defects, honoured by
scripts/sarif-gate.py in the CodeQL and Trivy jobs of .github/workflows/ci.yml.
This is not a way to stop seeing a finding. An accepted finding is still listed in the job
summary, with the reason below beside it, so a reviewer sees what the gate did not stop on. What
the entry removes is the build failure, and only for the exact finding it describes.
Matching is on the rule, the file and a fragment of the message - never on a line number, which
moves with the next edit above it, and never on the file alone. A different finding of the same
rule in the same file is a different finding and fails the build until somebody reads it too.
An entry that matches nothing fails the build. That is the dangerous state: the finding it
described has been fixed or has changed, so the register would otherwise be accepting something
nobody has read. Remove the entry, or read the finding again.
There is a third cause, it cost two days, and it was misdiagnosed the first time, so it is written
down carefully. Until 2026-09-09 the CodeQL C# job ran with the action's diff-informed queries at
their default, which is on for a pull request and off for a push. On a pull request the action
restricted the alerts the queries produced to the lines that pull request touched - and because it
does that at query-evaluation time, the report this register is matched against was narrowed too. So
a finding in a file no pull request had touched was absent from every pull request report and present
in every push report, and one register could not be right for both.
On 2026-09-07 the two cs/cleartext-storage-of-sensitive-information entries below were removed as
stale on the strength of a pull request run, and the removal recorded the wrong reason: it blamed a
dependency bump for the findings no longer being produced. The evidence against that was already
there. The push run on 2f79e95, which carried that very bump, reported all nine findings and passed
with both entries accepted; the pull request run twenty-two minutes later, same scanner, same
byte-identical SessionService.cs, reported none and called them stale. The event differed, not the
dependencies. Seven minutes after the removal landed, `main` went red on the two findings and stayed
red for two days while every pull request went green - which is the shape of the problem, and why it
took two days to see.
.github/workflows/ci.yml now sets CODEQL_ACTION_DIFF_INFORMED_QUERIES to false so that a pull request
and a push scan and report the same tree, and the reason is written out there. Before removing an
entry as stale, check which event produced the report you are reading, and check whether the code the
entry names has actually changed; if it has not, the entry is almost certainly still right.
`scope` names the scan the entry belongs to, and the gate is given a --scope so it applies only
the entries written for the run in hand. It is not decoration: the CodeQL job is a matrix over
csharp and javascript-typescript, and without it a C# entry matches nothing on the JavaScript run
and fails it as stale - which is what happened the first time this was wired in.
The same field is what will let a Trivy finding live here beside a CodeQL one.
This register is for findings that are wrong. A finding that is right but is being carried
anyway is a different thing and belongs in docs/process/waivers.md, with an owner and an expiry.

accepted.reason: The value logged is the enum member SessionRotationReason.PasswordChanged — a reason code, not a credential. CodeQL's heuristic reads the identifier, sees 'Password', and treats the constant as sensitive data reaching a log sink. What the line actually writes is 'Rotated session X into Y because PasswordChanged', which is the audit trail this rotation exists to leave. Removed on 2026-09-07 as stale, on the strength of a pull request report that had been narrowed to that pull request's own diff and so could not contain it, and restored on 2026-09-09 once that was understood. The code it names has not changed a byte between the two dates, so this is the same reading it was accepted under rather than a new one.

The same heuristic on the same word, one type along: SessionEndReason.PasswordChanged is the reason every other session was revoked when somebody changed their password. The enum is persisted by name (IdentityDbContext maps it with HasConversion<string>), so the member is a stored reason code; renaming it to something without the word 'password' would be a data migration made to satisfy a scanner, and would make the vocabulary worse.
